clues.title: Camera: low-cam, big car blur, low viewpoint
text: By far the most important way to recognize Switzerland, is that all car coverage is **low-cam**. This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries. This can be recognized in two ways:
- The car blur is significantly bigger.
- Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle.
Generally, the bigger car blur is the most consistent way to recognize low-cam.

NOTE: The only other countries that always have low-cam are [Japan](https://www.google.com/maps/@35.8415638,139.9145236,3a,75y,305.11h,83.84t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sLyYnyrI7fgLeL5Ev09XeJg!2e0!6shttps:%2F%2Fstreetviewpixels-pa.googleapis.com%2Fv1%2Fthumbnail%3Fpanoid%3DLyYnyrI7fgLeL5Ev09XeJg%26cb_client%3Dmaps_sv.tactile.gps%26w%3D203%26h%3D100%26yaw%3D33.088177%26pitch%3D0%26thumbfov%3D100!7i16384!8i8192) and [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/jn7cXhtXQRG6Hd9a6).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: All car coverage is low-cam: the camera sits lower than usual, so the car blur is much bigger, roads look wider and things are seen from a low angle. Japan and Liechtenstein also always have this.

clues.title: Plate: all white, no blue strip, short front
text: Swiss **licence plates** differ substantially from other European plates. They are fully white and lack the blue strip found in most other European countries.
**Front plates** are extremely short compared to most in Europe.
**Rear plates** can be either long or tall. In both cases the red country emblem can be seen on the left, while the canton emblem can be seen on the right.

images.caption: Swiss plates: short front, long rear and high rear

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: All-white plates with no blue EU strip. The front plate is very short, and the rear is long or tall. A red country emblem is on the left and a canton emblem on the right.

clues.title: Bollard: black-white, wedge or round top
text: Swiss bollards are **black-and-white **with white or grey reflectors. They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.
NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical [round bollards](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JJSg67HrDHerzv8c7).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black and white bollards with white or grey reflectors, either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top. Liechtenstein has almost identical round ones.

clues.title: Sign: blue main-road
text: The colour of **directional signs** indicates which type of road you are on. Main road signs will be blue, while side roads are white.

Major place names will frequently appear on blue signs, while smaller places tend to be on white signs. However, you can still find large city names on a [white sign](https://goo.gl/maps/pfJ2QNrPFmB7q6xN9).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Direction sign colour tells the road type: blue for main roads and white for side roads. Big place names are often on blue, small ones on white, though big cities can appear on white too.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian crossing, seven stripes
text: Swiss pedestrian signs have **seven stripes**, making it almost unique for Europe. Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles.
NOTE: Liechtenstein uses identical signs.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A pedestrian sign with seven stripes, almost unique in Europe, shaped as a tall blue rectangle instead of the usual square. Liechtenstein uses identical signs.

clues.title: Road lines: long dashed yellow
text: **Long dashed yellow** road lines are a good clue for Switzerland.
NOTE: These road lines are also common in Liechtenstein.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Long dashed yellow road lines are a good clue. They are also common in Liechtenstein.

clues.title: Road: yellow-painted pedestrian crossings
text: Pedestrian crossings are typically painted **yellow** and exclusive to Switzerland and [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/WLYNNkZAGCz7rDLg8) within Europe.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yellow-painted crossings exist in Europe only here and in Liechtenstein.

clues.title: Sign: round grey metal border on direction
text: Swiss road signs commonly have a round, grey **metal border** around them.

NOTE: [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wbSfjB8xPexuUkqZA) uses almost identical directional signs. Somewhat similar metal borders are found on some directional signs in [Denmark](https://goo.gl/maps/gQWu5BCRsga8WkiS7).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Road signs commonly have a round grey metal border. Liechtenstein's direction signs are nearly identical, and Denmark has somewhat similar metal borders on some.

differs.how: Only some direction signs have similar metal borders

clues.title: Sign: white or blue town entry, metal frame
text: Town entry signs in Switzerland are usually **white or blue**, with a **metal frame** around them.

NOTE: On the back of these signs you may often find the distance to larger, nearby cities. Furthermore, the abbreviation for the canton can often be seen on the bottom of the sign, especially when the town is situated near a canton border.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Town entry signs are usually white or blue with a metal frame. The back often shows distances to nearby big cities, and the bottom often shows the canton abbreviation, especially near canton borders.

clues.title: Chevron: black with white arrow
text: **Chevrons** are black with a white arrow. You may also rarely find chevrons that are [white with a black arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/S8YmmUW2vnbEQryN9).
NOTE: Austrian chevrons are red and white, or red and yellow.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black chevrons with a white arrow, rarely white with a black arrow. Austrian chevrons are red and white or red and yellow.

differs.how: Austrian chevrons are red and white or red and yellow

clues.title: Landscape: very mountainous south
text: While the southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, with long, thin valleys between the mountains, the northern half mostly consists of large farmlands on either flat ground or rolling hills, typically with forested hills in the distance.

images.caption: Four views: ploughed field, green meadow, snowy mountains and a winding mountain road

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The south is extremely mountainous with long thin valleys. The north is mostly big farmland on flat or rolling ground, with forested hills in the distance.

clues.title: Houses: warm-coloured stone, wood, shutters
text: Swiss and Alpine architecture in general largely consists of **stone buildings** painted in light and warm colours, often combined with wooden parts and details. Roofs are typically tiled and of a gable type. It is extremely common for windows to have wooden shutters which open horizontally in two parts.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Stone buildings in light, warm colours with wooden parts and details, tiled gable roofs, and wooden shutters that open horizontally in two halves.

clues.title: Sign: bus stop with thick metal post around it
text: These bus stop signs, with thick **metal signposts** going around them, are unique to Switzerland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bus stop signs with a thick metal post going around them, unique to this country.

clues.title: Language: four languages by region
text: Switzerland has **four official languages**: German, French, Italian and [Romansh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romansh_language), which are spoken in the regions shown. Note that some areas, mostly near the region borders, are bilingual.
NOTE: Unlike Germany and Austria, Swiss German does not use the letter **ß**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: German, French, Italian and Romansh are spoken in their own regions, with some bilingual areas near borders. Unlike Germany and Austria, Swiss German doesn't use ß.

differs.how: Swiss German has no ß; Germany uses it
Swiss German has no ß; Austria uses it

clues.title: Sign: speed limit wording follows regional
text: The text on the **speed limit signs** varies depending on the official languages in the region.

images.caption: Swiss speed sign wording by language region: Generell, Limite générale, Limite generale and limita generala

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The text on speed limit signs changes with the official language of the region.

clues.title: Sign: two-letter canton abbreviations
text: **Cantons** are the first-level administrative division of Switzerland. It is very common to find the two-letter abbreviation for the canton that you are in, as seen on some town entry signs. As such, remembering these can be a great asset when region-guessing Switzerland.
NOTE: If you happen to come across an [unblurred licence plate](https://maps.app.goo.gl/yi7rVDEFGXqwZaWSA), the first two letters will correspond to the canton that it is registered in.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The two-letter abbreviation of the canton often shows on town entry signs, so learning them helps region-guessing. An unblurred plate starts with the canton letters.

clues.title: Postal codes: first digits rise west to east
text: The first digits of Swiss postal codes are a good way to regionguess the country. The general pattern is that the numbers increase from the west to east.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The first digits of postal codes are a good region clue. They generally increase from west to east.

clues.title: Landscape: mountainous south, lower north
text: **Elevation** is an important part of region-guessing Switzerland. The southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, while the northern half mostly has smaller mountains and hills.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Elevation is key. The south is extremely mountainous, while the north mostly has smaller mountains and hills.

clues.title: Landscape: flat land
text: A fairly flat landscape with a long chain of medium-sized, forested mountains northwest means you are likely south of the Jura Mountains.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A fairly flat landscape with a long chain of medium forested mountains to the northwest means you are likely south of the Jura mountains.

clues.title: Landscape: limestone cliffs poking from
text: **Exposed limestone rocks**, protruding from forested hills, are commonly found in the Jura mountains.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Exposed limestone rocks sticking out of forested hills are common in the Jura mountains.

clues.title: Landscape: rock walls, mostly Jura
text: **Rock walls** are mainly found in the Jura mountains, but can also be found in the Alps, particularly in the Italian speaking parts.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Rock walls are mainly in the Jura mountains, but also in the Alps, particularly in the Italian-speaking parts.

clues.title: Houses: smooth orange-yellow stone
text: Not unexpectedly, seeing typical **Italian architecture** in Switzerland should imply that you are in the Italian-speaking areas in the south, principally the canton of Ticino.

The architectural style is characterized by, typically very smooth, orange-yellow stone walls with multiple floors and orange or brownish tiled roofs. Green and brown Italian-style window shutters are common.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Italian-style architecture means the Italian-speaking south, mainly Ticino: very smooth orange-yellow stone walls, several floors, orange or brown tiled roofs, and green or brown shutters.

clues.title: Houses: big, thick roofs arched underneath
text: Large houses with thick roofs, which are shaped like an **arch** **underneath**, are common around Bern.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Large houses with thick roofs that curve like an arch underneath are common around Bern.

clues.title: Houses: elaborate red timber frames, northeast
text: **Elaborate timber frames**, which are commonly painted red, are found in the northeast.
NOTE: [Simpler timber frames](https://maps.app.goo.gl/8cAS5uQ6KW7MVwux9) in other colours can be found in other parts of the country.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Elaborate timber frames, often painted red, are in the northeast. Simpler timber frames in other colours appear elsewhere.

clues.title: Houses: living house joined to barn at 90
text: Around Appenzell, most houses will consist of a large living house connected to a long barn, such that the roof of the living house and the barn are at a **90° angle**.
The front facade of the living house will often be divided into small squares, with each window being perfectly contained within a square.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Around Appenzell, a large living house is joined to a long barn at a right angle, with the house front split into small squares each holding a window.

clues.title: Houses: all-stone with white painted trim
text: In the canton of Graubünden, you will often come across houses entirely made of stone, with, most commonly white, **decorative painted details** around windows and the edges of the house.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Graubünden, houses entirely of stone with mostly white decorative painted details around windows and edges.

clues.title: Sign: large town entry signs
text: These **large** town entry signs can sometimes be found in the canton of Vaud.

images.caption: Town entry signs with a round 50 plate above the place name

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: These large town entry signs are sometimes seen in the canton of Vaud.

clues.title: Sign: olive green posts, borders and backs
text: **Olive green infrastructure**, particularly signposts, sign borders and sign backs, are found in Basel-Landschaft.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Olive green signposts, sign borders and sign backs are found in Basel-Landschaft.

clues.title: Bollard: thick wooden, square or round
text: In the canton of Valais, you will often see thick wooden bollards, which can either be **square-shaped** or **cylindrical**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In the canton of Valais, thick wooden bollards, square or cylindrical, are common.

clues.title: Bollard: reflectors on roadside fences instead
text: In place of bollards, reflectors in the canton of Glarus will often be **attached to fences** following the road.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Glarus, reflectors are often attached to fences along the road instead of bollards.

clues.title: Road: bike symbol with simple person on two
text: In Geneva and in the valley between Martigny and Lake Geneva, you can find bike path symbols painted on the road with a **simplified person** on top of two **disconnected wheels**.
NOTE: This stands in contrast to the rest of the country, where the symbol will be a [somewhat detailed bike](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1zfGBch8koTPW4pLA).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Around Geneva and in the valley between Martigny and Lake Geneva, the painted bike symbol is a simple person on top of two separate wheels. Elsewhere it's a more detailed bike.

clues.title: Road dividers: types by region (graphic)
text: You may find several different types of **road dividers** across the country, distributed as seen in this graphic.
_This image was provided by quarksauce. You can click on the image to enlarge it._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Several kinds of road dividers appear across the country, with distribution shown in the graphic (by quarksauce). Click to enlarge.

clues.title: Landscape: hilly, big lake south
text: If the area around your location appears hilly, but not mountainous, and you manage to catch a glimpse of a large lake to the south, with **tall mountains** on the other side, then you are very likely north of Lake Geneva.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Hilly but not mountainous land, with a large lake to the south and tall mountains on the far side, means you are very likely north of Lake Geneva.

clues.title: Landscape: wide lake northeast, low terrain
text: Seeing a wide lake to the northeast, situated in a landscape with relatively low elevation, means you should be looking at **Lake Constance **(on some Maps labelled as the Bodensee).
NOTE: Due to the low-lying landscape, you will probably be fairly close to the shore if you see the lake.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A wide lake to the northeast in fairly low land is Lake Constance (Bodensee). You are probably close to the shore.

clues.title: Plants: many small fruit trees in a wide flat
text: The valley of Martigny has the highest density of **fruit plantations** in the country. It can easily be recognized by the many small fruit trees in combination with the wide, flat valley with large mountains on either side.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Martigny valley has the most fruit plantations in the country: lots of small fruit trees in a wide, flat valley with big mountains either side.

clues.title: Plants: fruit trees near big lakes
text: Apart from the valley of Martigny, the most likely area to find **fruit trees** is near Lake Constance, followed by the area northwest of Lake Geneva.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Outside the Martigny valley, fruit trees are most likely near Lake Constance, then northwest of Lake Geneva.

clues.title: Coverage: train coverage on a mountain railway
text: In the canton of Graubünden, you can find this unique and easily recognizable **train coverage** on the tracks of the “Bernina Express.” It runs around most of the canton, all the way down to Tirano in Italy.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Graubünden, distinctive train coverage on the Bernina Express tracks, running around most of the canton down to Tirano in Italy.

clues.title: Google car: rare Gen 2, near two cantons
text: **Generation 2** coverage is very limited in Switzerland. It can be found mostly near the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais, and on a few very short stretches in Schaffhausen.
NOTE: This does not include the many ski resorts with Generation 2 snow coverage, which can be found throughout the southern half of the country.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The older Gen 2 camera (lower quality) is very limited: mostly near the Bern-Valais border and a few short stretches in Schaffhausen. Ski resorts with Gen 2 snow coverage are not counted.

clues.title: Sign: blue street name with rounded side edges
text: These blue street signs, with **rounded edges** on the sides, are unique to the city of Sankt Gallen.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Blue street signs with rounded edges on the sides, unique to Sankt Gallen.

clues.title: Sign: large blue street name on low double post
text: Large blue street signs, attached to a **low double signpost**, similar to directional signs in [Denmark](https://maps.app.goo.gl/234Fd9GSuZQRtH47A), are found in Basel.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Large blue street signs on a low double signpost, like Danish direction signs, in Basel.

differs.how: Danish direction signs look similar but are not street names

clues.title: Houses: grey four-floor buildings
text: Downtown Bern can be recognized by this **specific architecture**. Grey toned buildings, typically with four floors and large, somewhat rounded openings lined up on the ground floor are common.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Downtown Bern: grey-toned buildings, usually four floors, with large, somewhat rounded openings lined up along the ground floor.

clues.title: Sign: speed limit "limite generale"
text: Italian is spoken in the southern part of Switzerland near the border with Italy. Look for speed limit signs that say "limite generale".

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Italian is spoken in the south near Italy. Speed signs saying "limite generale" show you are in the Italian-speaking part.

clues.title: Sign: speed limit "limite générale"
text: The west part of Switzerland bordering France speaks French. One of the most helfpul metas is to look for speed limit signs that say "limite générale"

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: French is spoken in the west. Speed signs saying "limite générale" (with accent) show you are in the French-speaking part.

clues.title: Language: Romansh words like ospidal, scoula
text: Romansh is a language spoken in parts of western Switzerland. You will often find it mixed in with German (and possibly Italian). Most helpful may be to learn a few words that you may see and recognize that if you are in Switzerland but it's not one of the other 3 languages it's Romansh.
**ospidal** - hospital
**scoula** - school
**bainvgnieu** - welcome
**limita generala** - speed limit
**restorant** - restaurant
**parc naziunal** - national park
**svizzer** - switzerland
**attenziun** - warning

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A Romansh word mixed with German or Italian means Romansh country: ospidal (hospital), scoula (school), bainvgnieu (welcome), limita generala (speed limit), restorant, parc naziunal, attenziun (warning).

clues.title: Sign: blue street name, white edge, four dots
text: Zurich street signs are blue with a white edge and 4 thick dots in each corner.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Zurich street signs are blue with a white edge and four thick dots in the corners.

clues.title: Language: German region, ss instead of ß
text: Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. German is the most widely spoken language in Switzerland. It is (mostly) spoken in central and northern parts of the country. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.
NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.
ALSO NOTE: Unlike Germany and Austria, Swiss German does not use the letter **ß**, replacing it by **ss** in words like **Straße** (street), becoming **Strasse** in Swiss German.

images.caption: German text with Ä Ö Ü shown large, using ss instead of ß
Blue street sign reading Kirchenfeldstrasse, spelled with ss

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: German is the most spoken language, mostly in the centre and north. Place names on the map hint at the language. Swiss German writes ss instead of ß, so Strasse not Straße.

differs.how: Germany writes ß, Swiss German writes ss
Austria writes ß, Swiss German writes ss

clues.title: Language: French region in the west
text: Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. French is the second most spoken language in Switzerland after German. It is spoken in western parts of the country. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.
NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: French is the second most spoken language, in the west. Place names on the map hint at the language, and borders are sometimes bilingual.

clues.title: Language: Italian region in the south
text: Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. Italian is spoken in southern parts of the country, close to Italy. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.
NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Italian is spoken in the south, close to Italy. Place names on the map hint at the language, and borders are sometimes bilingual.

clues.title: Houses: wide, very low-pitched roofs
text: **Wide houses with strikingly low-pitched roofs** and often a **large number of windows** are frequently found in the **cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel**, as well as in the **northern part of the canton of Bern**. A variant with a **half-hipped roof** also exists.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Wide houses with strikingly low-pitched roofs and many windows, in the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel and the north of Bern. A half-hipped variant exists.

clues.title: Roofs: small bump finial on the ridge
text: **Finials** in the form of a **small bump on a roof** can be found in the areas shown on the map, being common in the cantons of **Vaud, Fribourg, Geneva** and **Neuchatel** and also in **western Valais**. They can also very rarely be found in the canton of Bern.

images.caption: Roof ridge with a small bump finial; the purple circle marks it

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A small bump-shaped finial on the roof, common in Vaud, Fribourg, Geneva, Neuchâtel and western Valais, very rarely in Bern.

clues.title: Roofs: chimney right by the gable end
text: Chimneys located on the **small gable roof of ​​half-hipped roofs** or **very close to the gable on hipped roofs** are particularly found in western Switzerland, especially in the cantons of **Vaud** and **Fribourg**, although exceptions can rarely be found elsewhere.

images.caption: Chimney right by the gable end, circled in purple

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Chimneys on the small gable of half-hipped roofs, or very near the gable on hipped roofs, mostly in the west (Vaud and Fribourg), with rare exceptions.

clues.title: Houses: low roof with balcony in the gable
text: In the **canton of Neuchâtel**, these wide houses with low-pitched roofs will sometimes have a **balcony integrated into the gable**. You will also sometimes see **wood-clad gable arches** on these houses.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Neuchâtel, wide low-roofed houses sometimes have a balcony built into the gable, and sometimes wood-clad gable arches.

clues.title: Houses: wide recessed entrance
text: A **devant-huis** is a **traditional, wide, recessed entranceway** of a building found in the **canton of Jura**. There will often be vertical timber plank cladding above the entrance.

images.caption: Wide recessed entrance, circled in purple on the left

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A devant-huis is a traditional wide, recessed entranceway in the canton of Jura, often with vertical timber planks above the entrance.

clues.title: Houses: arched gates, now flats or shops
text: Houses with **arched gates** can be found in the **north and west of the country** as shown on the map. Traditionally serving as entrances to farmhouses and barns, they now often conceal modern apartments, shops or restaurants.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Houses with arched gates in the north and west, once entrances to farmhouses and barns, now often hiding modern flats, shops or restaurants.

clues.title: Houses: wide tent-like roofs with deep overhang
text: **Strikingly wide houses resembling tents**, with **deeply overhanging roofs** and a bulky overall appearance, can be found in the **northern half of the canton of Bern**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Strikingly wide, bulky houses with deeply overhanging tent-like roofs, in the northern half of the canton of Bern.

clues.title: Houses: half-hipped roof
text: In the **canton of Bern** and neighbouring cantons, houses featuring half-hipped roofs with a **thick arch under the gable**, giving the house a bulky appearance, can be found.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Half-hipped roofs with a thick arch under the gable, giving a bulky look, in Bern and neighbouring cantons.

clues.title: Walls: pale yellow bricks, west to east strip
text: **Pale yellow bricks** are found in a broad strip stretching **from Bern in the west to St. Gallen in the east**. Buildings can be entirely constructed from these bricks . However, you can also often see the bricks used in conjunction with **decorative red bricks** and in otherwise wooden buildings.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Pale yellow bricks in a wide strip from Bern to St. Gallen. Houses can be all brick or mix them with red decorative bricks or timber.

clues.title: Houses: wavy gable arches
text: Gables in the **canton of Lucerne** commonly have arches similar to those you see in the canton of Bern. However unlike the simple semicircular arches in Bern, the **arches** are **undulating**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Gables in Lucerne have arches like those in Bern, but wavy instead of simple semicircles.

clues.title: Walls: miniature roofs over windows
text: Houses with **‘miniature roofs' over windows** are found in the area shown on the map. Sometimes these ‘miniature roofs' will span the whole wall and sometimes just the windows below them .

images.caption: Miniature roof over a window, circled in purple

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Houses with tiny roofs over windows, in the area on the map. Sometimes they run along the whole wall, sometimes just over the windows.

clues.title: Walls: irregular stones smeared with light
text: Buildings with walls made of **irregular stones plastered with a thick, light-coloured mortar**, often smeared over the stones, are found in **Valais**, **Ticino** and the **Italian-speaking parts of Grisons**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Walls of irregular stone plastered with thick, light mortar smeared over the stones, in Valais, Ticino and the Italian-speaking parts of Graubünden.

clues.title: Houses: several small roofs on the gable end
text: Houses featuring **multiple small roofs on the gable end** can be found in the areas shown on the map, although can exceptionally be found elsewhere. The small roofs will sometimes also continue along the side walls of the building.

images.caption: Several small roofs on the gable end; the purple circle marks one over a window

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Several small roofs on the gable end, in the mapped areas (rarely elsewhere). They can continue along the side walls.

clues.title: Walls: wooden shingle cladding
text: Traditional **wooden shingle wall cladding** is found across a central belt stretching **from the canton of St. Gallen in the east to Valais in the west**. The shapes of the shingles can vary and may be rounded or angular .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Traditional wooden shingle walls in a central belt from St. Gallen in the east to Valais in the west. Shingles can be rounded or angular.

clues.title: Walls: pastel-coloured shingles
text: **Shingle walls in a range of pastel colours** are found primarily in **the east of the country**, becoming less common towards the west, although can be occasionally found anywhere. The shape of shingles can vary: round , rectangular , diamond and cone shapes all exist.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Shingle walls in pastel colours, mostly in the east and rarer towards the west. Shingles can be round, rectangular, diamond or cone shaped.

clues.title: Roofs: rectangular metal panels
text: In **Valais** and **Grisons, rectangular metal panels** are sometimes used to roof houses and sheds. They are particularly found in the **northwest of Grisons**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Rectangular metal panels sometimes roof houses and sheds in Valais and Graubünden, especially the northwest of Graubünden.

clues.title: Roofs: chimney at the gable end
text: In the valleys of **central Ticino**, you will find houses with **gable-end chimneys**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Houses with chimneys at the gable end are found in the central valleys of Ticino.

clues.title: Roofs: double pitch, lower part shallower
text: **Double-pitched gable roofs**, with the lower part of the roof at a shallower angle, can be seen in the area shown on the map.

images.caption: Double-pitch roof with a shallower lower part; the purple circle marks the lower slope

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Gable roofs in two slopes, with the lower part at a shallower angle, in the mapped area.

clues.title: Roofs: downward-pointing ends of beams
text: **Downward-pointing finials** at the ends of the load-bearing beams on gable roofs can be found in the areas shown on the map. They can take a variety of shapes, ranging from rectangular to ornamental forms.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Downward-pointing finials on the ends of the load-bearing beams of gable roofs, in the mapped areas. Shapes range from rectangular to ornamental.

clues.title: Houses: shutterless window rows with
text: A very distinctive style of house is found in the **Appenzell** cantons and neighbouring **St. Gallen**.
These houses have **rows of sets of shutterless windows** on the gable side of the house, with **rectangular panels** underneath and between the sets of windows.
A **‘baroque’ variant** of this style can be found, commonly in urban settings, with a distinctive curved roof shape and often decoration on the panels.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A distinctive house style in the Appenzell cantons and nearby St. Gallen: rows of shutterless windows on the gable side with rectangular panels beneath and between. A baroque variant in towns has a curved roof and decorated panels.

clues.title: Houses: timber frame, thick arches, tent roofs
text: **Timber frame houses** are found in two main regions of Switzerland as shown on the map. There are rare exceptions elsewhere.
In the **western distribution area**, you will often see timber frame houses with **thick arched gables , triangular timber supports under the roof**, and **large tent roofs**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Timber-frame houses occur in two main regions. In the west they often have thick arched gables, triangular supports under the roof and big tent roofs.

clues.title: Roofs: very flat, barely sloped
text: Most houses in **Valsot**, in the extreme east of the country, have **very flat roofs** with a barely noticeable slope. These houses can also be found in other nearby villages.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Most houses in Valsot in the far east have very flat roofs with a barely visible slope, and nearby villages too.

clues.title: Houses: timber frame, double-pitch, big dormers
text: **Timber frame houses** are found in two main regions of Switzerland as shown on the map. There are rare exceptions elsewhere.

In the **northeastern distribution area**, common features of timber frame houses include **double-pitched gable roofs** and **large dormers** . Additionally these houses can sometimes take the form of **long buildings running lengthwise along the street** .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In the northeastern timber-frame region: double-pitched gable roofs, big dormers, and sometimes long buildings running along the street.

clues.title: Roofs: slate in neat rows
text: In **Ticino**, slate roofs will sometimes be organised in **neat rows of slate tiles**, as opposed to the less regular pattern normal on other slate-roofed houses in Switzerland.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Ticino slate roofs are sometimes laid in neat rows, unlike the more irregular pattern on other Swiss slate roofs.

clues.title: Roofs: slate, three southern cantons
text: **Slate roofs** are commonly found in the three southern cantons of **Valais**, **Ticino**, and **Grisons**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Slate roofs are common in the three southern cantons: Valais, Ticino and Graubünden.

clues.title: Walls: sgraffito patterns carved in plaster
text: In **Grisons**, you will find the traditional decorative technique known as **sgraffito**, where intricate patterns or motifs are carved into the fresh, light lime plaster of house facades to reveal the darker layer of plaster beneath.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Graubünden, sgraffito: patterns carved into fresh light plaster to show the darker layer beneath.

clues.title: Walls: more colourful sgraffito
text: **Val Müstair**, in the far east of Grisons, paints its houses with a unique variant of Grisons **sgraffito** with **more colours** and **a different style of designs**. Normal sgraffito can also be found here

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Val Müstair in the far east of Graubünden paints houses in a variant of sgraffito with more colours and different designs. Normal sgraffito also occurs.

clues.title: Houses: tall, narrow dark wood with balconies
text: **Dark-wood houses** in the mountainous north-south valleys of **Valais** are comparatively **tall and narrow**.

Often **roofed with slate tiles**, these houses frequently feature **multiple balconies** and **decorative wooden fretwork**. **Interlocking log joints**, a typical feature of the region, are usually visible at the corners of the houses.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In the north-south valleys of Valais, dark-wood houses are tall and narrow, often slate-roofed with several balconies, decorative fretwork and visible interlocking log corners.

clues.title: Houses: dark wood with a curved support under
text: In **Obwalden and surrounding areas**, you can find dark-wood houses (in varying styles) with a structural curve along the length of a wall supporting a cantilevered upper storey . This upper storey sometimes includes a balcony.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Obwalden and nearby, dark-wood houses have a curved structural support along a wall holding up an overhanging upper floor, sometimes with a balcony.

clues.title: Houses: wide dark wood, carved dates
text: **Dark-wood houses** that are **particularly wide** can be seen in the southern parts of the **cantons of Bern** and **Vaud** and in **northwestern Valais**.
Common features of these houses include:
**wood carvings** and **inscriptions** with the year of construction or other text
**decorative soffits** can along the edge of the roof
either a **staircase** or **a pair of staircases**
**covered balconies and verandas on the side of the house**.
You can also see **timber versions** of the **thick arched roofs** common in this area.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Wide dark-wood houses in southern Bern and Vaud and northwest Valais, with carvings and inscriptions (e.g. build year), decorated eaves, one or two staircases, covered side balconies, and wooden versions of the thick arched roofs.

clues.title: Roofs: large diamond-shaped slate slabs
text: Roofs featuring **large, diamond-shaped, slate slabs** are found across **central Valais**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Roofs with large diamond-shaped slate slabs, across central Valais.

clues.title: Walls: timber and white plaster
text: Houses blending **timber** and **white-plastered walls** are most common in **Valais** and **northern Grisons**, typically following a one-third to two-thirds ratio of either material.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Houses mixing timber and white plaster, usually one-third of one and two-thirds of the other, most common in Valais and northern Graubünden.

clues.title: Barns: wavy or semicircular gable arch
text: Similar to houses in the region, barns in the **canton of Lucerne** can feature an **undulating gable arch**, or, unlike the houses, a **semicircular gable arch**.
Barns in this area may also have a distinctive style of **half-hipped roof with a tiny triangular gable**.
Variants of these barns exist with an entrance for vehicle access .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Barns in Lucerne can have a wavy gable arch or, unlike houses, a semicircular one. Some have a half-hipped roof with a tiny triangular gable, and some a vehicle entrance.

clues.title: Barns: gable covered in terracotta or grey
text: In **western Fribourg**, you can find barns with **gables** that are clad with either **terracotta-coloured tiles** or occasionally **grey, diamond-shaped ones**.
A variant of these barns also exists with an additional entrance for vehicle access .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In western Fribourg, barns with gables covered in terracotta tiles or sometimes grey diamond-shaped ones. A variant has an extra vehicle entrance.

clues.title: Barns: low-pitched roofs like local houses
text: Barns **in the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel** often have **low-pitched roofs**, mirroring the design of local houses.
The barns often form part of the same building as the main house, although can be separate. Either version may feature large double doors for vehicle access .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Barns in Jura and Neuchâtel often have low-pitched roofs like local houses, usually part of the same building but sometimes separate, with large double doors for vehicles.

clues.title: Barns: wide with tent-like roofs
text: Strikingly wide barns with tent-like roofs, resembling those found on houses in the region, can be found in the northern half of the canton of Bern.A variant of these barns exists with an additional covered entrance allowing vehicle access.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Strikingly wide barns with tent-like roofs, like local houses, in the northern half of Bern. A variant has a covered vehicle entrance.

clues.title: Barns: house and barn fused together
text: In the **Entlebuch region**, in the far south of the **canton of Lucerne**, you can find **‘cyborg’ house-barns** with the house and barn ‘fused’ together. These buildings are particularly striking when viewed from the front .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In the Entlebuch region, the far south of Lucerne, house and barn are fused into one building, especially striking from the front.

clues.title: Houses: gables covered with red tiles
text: Houses with **gables covered with striking red tiles** are frequently found in **northeastern Vaud** and **the west of the canton of Fribourg**. In exceptional cases, similar tiled gables can be found outside these regions however.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Houses with gables covered in striking red tiles are frequent in northeastern Vaud and western Fribourg, with rare cases elsewhere.

clues.title: Barns: double-pitch roof, lower part shallower
text: Like houses in the same region, barns in the area shown on the map can sometimes have **double-pitched gable roofs**, with the lower part of the roof at a shallower angle.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Barns in the mapped area can have double-pitched roofs, the lower part at a shallower angle, like houses nearby.

clues.title: Barns: bulky, half-hipped, timber supports
text: In the canton of **Bern**, the design of barns generally mirrors the local architecture. Barns in this region are typically **bulky in appearance** and frequently have **half-hipped roofs**. The roofs may also feature timber supports.
A variant exists with an additional entrance for vehicle access. Sometimes the barn will be directly attached to the house .

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Bern, barns mirror local houses: bulky, often half-hipped roofs, sometimes timber supports. A variant has a vehicle entrance, and sometimes the barn attaches directly to the house.

clues.title: Barns: attached to house in T or L shape
text: Barns in **Appenzell** and the surrounding area are often **directly attached to the main house in a T-shaped or L-shaped layout**, making them often easy to recognise from a distance.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Barns in Appenzell and around are often attached to the house in a T or L layout, easy to spot from far away.

clues.title: Barns: prominent transverse roof below the
text: In **Zug **and neighbouring cantons, you can find barns with a **prominent transverse roof** extending below the main gable.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Zug and neighbouring cantons, barns with a prominent transverse roof extending below the main gable.

clues.title: Barns: diamond lattice pattern on doors
text: This **diamond lattice pattern** on the doors of barns is found in the **cantons of Thurgau and Zurich**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A diamond lattice pattern on barn doors, found in Thurgau and Zurich.

clues.title: Barns: wood with concrete or stone corners
text: Barns featuring a **combination of wood** and either **concrete or stone** can be found in **Valais** and **Grisons**. Typically, the concrete or stone elements are located at the corners of the barns. As with huts, **exposed round beams** are only found in Grisons.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Barns mixing wood with concrete or stone, usually at the corners, in Valais and Graubünden. Exposed round beams only occur in Graubünden.

clues.title: Huts: interlocking rectangular logs
text: The walls of **wooden huts** in **Valais** are often made from **a system of interlocking rectangular logs**, easily visible from the outside of the building.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Wooden huts in Valais are often built from interlocking rectangular logs visible from outside.

clues.title: Granary: raised wooden barn on stilts with
text: **Raccards** are the **traditional raised wooden granaries** of Valais. They are generally built on **short stilts** with a round stone slab on each stilt to guard against rodents.

images.caption: Circled detail of the raised wooden granary on stilts

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Raccards are raised wooden granaries of Valais, on short stilts each topped with a round stone slab to keep rodents out.

clues.title: Huts: round beams
text: A key feature of huts in **Grisons** is the frequent use of **round beams**, rather than rectangular ones, either for the overall structure or just in the gable area . Huts with just rectangular beams can still be seen in this area.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Huts in Graubünden often use round beams, for the whole structure or just the gable. Huts with rectangular beams also exist there.

clues.title: Huts: mainly stone, slate roofs
text: **Huts** in **Ticino** often have **stone** as their primary building material, with their roofs often made from **slate tiles**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Huts in Ticino are often mainly stone, with roofs of slate tiles.

clues.title: Barns: wooden upper-floor balconies
text: These **upper-floor wooden balconies** are commonly seen on barns in **southwestern Valais**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Upper-floor wooden balconies are common on barns in southwestern Valais.

clues.title: Shrines: colourful Catholic shrines
text: Catholic shrines in **Ticino** will often be **colourful** and feature **religious imagery**. Shrines in this area may also have **slate roofs**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Catholic shrines in Ticino are often colourful with religious imagery, and may have slate roofs.

clues.title: Churches: onion-shaped gable around the clock
text: Church towers featuring an **onion-shaped gable structure around a clock face** can be found in a central band from the canton of Bern in the west to Glarus in the east.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Church towers with an onion-shaped gable around the clock face, in a central band from Bern in the west to Glarus in the east.

clues.title: Churches: main spire with several small spires
text: Church towers featuring **multiple small spires** surrounding a main spire are most common in the west of the country, particularly around **Neuchâtel**, although they can occasionally be seen elsewhere

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Church towers with a main spire surrounded by small spires, most common in the west, especially around Neuchâtel, occasionally elsewhere.

clues.title: Churches: onion domes
text: Churches with **onion domes** are a strong indicator for the **non-French-speaking regions** of Switzerland, although exceptions exist elsewhere.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Onion domes on churches are a strong sign of the non-French-speaking regions, with exceptions.

clues.title: Churches: rooster on the steeple
text: A **rooster on top of a church steeple** usually signifies a Protestant church and is a strong indicator for the **French-speaking part of the country**, although isolated examples can be found elsewhere.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A rooster atop a church steeple usually means a Protestant church and strongly suggests the French-speaking part, with isolated exceptions.

clues.title: Churches: simple triangular gable tower
text: Church towers with a **simple triangular gable shape** are most frequently found in **northern and central Switzerland**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Church towers with a simple triangular gable are most frequent in the north and centre.

clues.title: Churches: tower with triangular gables on
text: Church towers where the tower walls form **triangular gables**, pointing up, on **multiple sides**, occur most frequently in the **northeast**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Church towers whose walls form upward-pointing triangular gables on several sides, most often in the northeast.
